analysis.one_liner: Restores and strengthens federal protections against workplace discrimination that the Supreme Court had cut back.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 273-158 with help from 22 Republicans, but the Senate never brought it to a vote; it was indefinitely postponed by unanimous consent on November 22, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After a string of 1989 Supreme Court decisions narrowed federal employment discrimination law, this bill wrote the old, broader protections back into statute. It put the burden of proof back on employers to justify hiring practices that fall more heavily on women and minorities, allowed compensatory and punitive damages and jury trials in intentional-discrimination cases, lengthened the time workers have to file complaints, and extended the same rules to employees of Congress itself. It also created a Glass Ceiling Commission to study barriers to advancing women and minorities and a Labor Department program on pay equity.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination on the job, especially women and minorities. The bill would have made it easier to win cases where a seemingly neutral practice (like a test or a seniority rule) has a discriminatory effect, because the employer — not the worker — would have to prove the practice is genuinely necessary for the job. It would have added money damages, including punitive damages capped at $150,000, and jury trials for intentional discrimination, extended the filing window from 180 to 540 days, restored protections for on-the-job bias in contracts that the Court had stripped away, and extended anti-discrimination coverage to congressional employees and to U.S. citizens working abroad for American companies.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-1989 rule that once an employee shows a hiring practice has a discriminatory effect, the employer must prove it is required by 'business necessity,' overruling the Supreme Court's Wards Cove decision that put that burden on the worker.
Allows compensatory damages, punitive damages capped at $150,000, and jury trials in cases of intentional discrimination — remedies that previously did not exist under Title VII.

Extends the deadline for filing a discrimination charge from 180 days to 540 days, and makes clear that an 1866 civil rights law covers bias on the job, not just in hiring, reversing Patterson v. McLean Credit Union.
Applies federal anti-discrimination law to employees of the House, Senate, and congressional agencies for the first time, and to U.S. citizens employed overseas.

Creates a Glass Ceiling Commission to study barriers to advancing women and minorities into executive positions and a Labor Department pay-equity program, and requires EEOC reporting on employment data by sex, race, and national origin.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — companies, unions, and employment agencies — would bear the cost. The bill restores their exposure to disparate-impact lawsuits, shifts the burden of proof onto them, adds compensatory and punitive damages and jury trials, and extends fee awards to include expert fees and litigation expenses. Those costs could show up in litigation spending and, in contested cases, settlements or judgments.

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection, voiced by business groups and President Bush at the time, was that the restored burden of proof and new damages would pressure employers into settling questionable claims to avoid large jury awards — critics called it a step toward racial quotas, though the bill's text expressly declares quotas an unlawful employment practice and defines them as fixed racial or gender targets.

The new damages and jury-trial rights apply only to intentional discrimination and are capped at $150,000, limits supporters accepted to win support — meaning victims of some serious bias still could not recover damages under this provision.

An honest supporter would acknowledge real costs: expanded liability and litigation expenses for employers of every size, some of which are passed to employees and consumers, and a heavier caseload for courts and the EEOC.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for workers are substantial: it restores protections that had been the law for two decades before the 1989 Court decisions and adds real remedies — damages, jury trials, a longer filing window — for discrimination victims. The costs are real but bounded: damages apply only to intentional discrimination, punitive damages are capped, and the bill explicitly outlaws quotas and preserves employer job requirements. On balance a serious attempt to rebalance employment discrimination law toward workers, with concessions built in.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 273-158, but the Senate simply put it on its calendar and, in November, quietly shelved it by unanimous consent — a routine objection-free move that killed it without anyone having to vote against it on the record. A negotiated compromise version was signed into law days earlier, so most of this bill's substance became law in a different vehicle.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to both the Judiciary and Education and Labor committees, which held multiple hearings and reported it to the House in the spring of 1991.
On June 5, 1991, the House passed the bill 273-158, with 250 of 266 voting Democrats in favor and 22 of 165 voting Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill in June and placed it on its legislative calendar, but never took it up; on November 22, 1991, the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The delay was mostly symbolic: a compromise civil rights bill was enacted the same month, so workers got most of the restored protections. What the Senate's shelving of this version avoided was the House's stronger remedies — the $150,000 punitive damages cap in the compromise was keyed to employer size and lower — so employers ended up somewhat better off under the enacted compromise than they would have under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who got a milder compromise instead

for.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed it through House passage.

for.name: House Education and Labor Committee and House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked up the bill, and reported it amended to the House.

for.name: 175 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 166 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

against.name: The Senate
against.role: Republican-held chamber under a Republican president
against.what_they_did: Left the House bill on its calendar for five months, then indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent without a vote.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the House-passed version, having vetoed a similar bill the year before over fears it would lead to quotas, and pushed a narrower compromise that was enacted instead.

against.name: Business and employer coalitions
against.role: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied employer groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill's burden-of-proof and damages provisions, arguing they would expose employers to quota-driven litigation.

sides.party_line_note: In the House the vote was 273-158: 250 of 266 voting Democrats (94%) in favor versus only 22 of 165 voting Republicans (13%).

industries.industry: Private employers (companies with 15 or more employees)
industries.note: The bill restores employer liability for facially neutral practices that disproportionately screen out women and minorities, shifts the burden of proof to the employer, and adds compensatory and punitive damages plus jury trials. Its interest in limiting lawsuits and damages runs against workers' ability to enforce anti-discrimination rights.

industries.industry: Employment discrimination plaintiffs' attorneys and litigation services
industries.note: New damages, jury trials, expert-fee awards, and a longer filing window would expand the market for discrimination cases. Workers and the bar gain together here, though it also raises employer litigation costs.

The bill tightens rules — tests must validly and fairly predict job performance regardless of race, sex, or national origin — and bans adjusting scores or cutoffs by race or sex, but also clarifies that professionally developed ability tests remain lawful, giving testing firms clearer rules in both directions.
